solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Luvvy's hot in plastic panties

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other
plastic can be moulded into any shape, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style snigger about an actor wearing hot plastic underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The underwear letters are rearranged to TESPIAN and the H slips in after the T. 'Luvvy's' reads as possessive but is 'Luvvy is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Luvvy is British slang, usually mocking, for an effusive actor, and a thespian is a formal word for an actor.

clue.text: Critic of vasectomy performer: "top of penis has been removed!"

indicators.note: something removed is taken away, so a letter comes out of the longer word

parts.note: a vasectomy is colloquially 'the snip', so the surgeon is a snipper

indicators.note: the top of a word written downward is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A surgeon who does vasectomies complains that the tip of a penis has been lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking one P out of SNIPPER leaves SNIPER; the colon makes the rest look like a quotation, but it is all wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniper, figuratively, is someone who takes potshots of criticism from a safe distance.

clue.text: Brenda, cutting into almost all of penis: "One has to be forceful"

indicators.note: a thing cutting into another ends up inside it
almost all means everything bar the final bit, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a vulgar slang word for penis, losing its last letter
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina, whose cipher is ER
I've, the contraction of 'I have', with one as I

explanation.surface: The Queen, interrupting a ruder topic, declares in her regal 'one' that one must be firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One has' sounds like royal speech but is a contraction with one as I. Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and her cipher stands for Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Coercive describes using force or threats to make someone comply, which matches the idea of being forceful.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) What the Coalition needs to succeed is part-time nuts

definitions.text: What the Coalition needs to succeed

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters have gone haywire and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A political jibe: whatever the Coalition needs to work, part-time involvement is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' belongs to the letters being rearranged, not the link. The Coalition is the 2010-15 Conservative and Liberal Democrat government of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Team spirit is the shared willingness of members to cooperate, which a two-party government needs in order to work.

clue.text: Pet area of genitalia, follow?

parts.note: the lap is the region where the genitals sit when seated
to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether a pet should follow someone's groin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like a verb in the surface but is the noun definition; the lap is euphemistically near the genitals.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapdog is a small dog kept as a pet and held on the owner's lap.

clue.text: Ready for that disaster, working with Conservative and lousy Libdem leaders?

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
the standard abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so the opening letters of the words are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of three words

explanation.surface: Mocking the Coalition: are the Tories and dismal Liberal Democrats prepared for disaster?
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' looks like a link but its A starts the run of leading letters; the 'disaster' is the Coalition itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor or engineer who is on call is available to respond immediately when an emergency arises.

clue.text: Electorate stuffed with Gordon's main lousy after-effect

indicators.note: something stuffed is filled, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the Electorate of Hanover was a German state whose ruler had a vote electing the Holy Roman Emperor

indicators.note: the main or chief part here is the leading letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Gordon

explanation.surface: Voters are fed up with Gordon Brown's legacy as a nasty aftermath of his time in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electorate' looks like the voters but is the historical German state, home of Britain's Georgian kings.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the unpleasant headache and nausea that follow heavy drinking, a nasty after-effect of the night before.

clue.text: New opening for "fatso" rear of Eamonn Holmes's support

indicators.note: a new opening replaces the first letter with a different one

parts.note: the insult with its F swapped for a W

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the name

explanation.surface: A jibe at Eamonn Holmes, a portly British TV presenter, about his weight and what holds him up.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes is swapped from the TV presenter to Sherlock; the replacement first letter is not clued, only signalled.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Watson is Sherlock Holmes's loyal companion and assistant in Conan Doyle's detective stories.

clue.text: Agency man, like, flips Thatcher's heart with one

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: as means like, as in 'as good as gold'

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the four central letters of Thatcher
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An adman, like, totally changes Thatcher's mind while working with a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Saatchi & Saatchi was the advertising agency behind Thatcher's 1979 'Labour isn't working' campaign, so the surface fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice and Charles Saatchi founded a famous London advertising agency, so either brother is an agency man.

clue.text: M'lud, rudely interrupting spiel, is a fruity, stodgy thing

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a puff is a piece of promotional patter, as is a spiel

indicators.note: doing something rudely means roughly, so these letters are roughed up

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A judge rudely interrupts a lawyer's speech, which turns out to be overripe and heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: M'lud is how British barristers address a judge. A puff is a promotional plug, so it fits spiel.
explanation.definitionFit: Plum duff is a traditional British suet pudding studded with raisins, both fruity and heavy.

clue.text: Drink taken by US TV show copper

parts.note: to sup is to drink in sips
ER is the American hospital drama

explanation.surface: A police officer from an American television series is having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'copper' suggests the metal or a coin, but here it is the British slang for police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A super is short for superintendent, a senior British police rank, and a copper is a police officer.

clue.text: Model stimulated on drive with a piece of ham

indicators.note: in an across clue, placed on means added after, so the following piece comes second
something stimulated is stirred up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
to ram something home is to drive it in
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashion model gets excited on a car journey while eating a ham sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ham' looks like meat, but it means overacting, and 'drive' is a verb rather than a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham acting is overwrought performance, and a melodrama is a play with exaggerated emotion, so it is a ham piece.

clue.text: Tumbledown remade as Iris (with nun)

indicators.note: something remade is put together afresh, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tumbledown, the Falklands War drama, remade with a different film starring a nun, Iris.
explanation.walkthrough: Tumbledown and Iris are both British films, which tempts a film-title answer; Tumbledown is just the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A building that is tumbledown is dilapidated and falling apart, which is what being in ruins describes.

clue.text: Foul curse — one heartless Tory's bond

indicators.note: foul means messed up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letters are cut out

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
the Conservative, losing its middle two letters

explanation.surface: Someone swears foully that a cruel Tory is bound up with them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory's' reads as possessive but just gives the word to be gutted; a Tory is a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: A bond is a financial instrument, a debt certificate, and such tradeable instruments are called securities.

clue.text: Fabulous 'snipped' organ on Cyclops put before the state

indicators.note: something snipped has been cut short, so the end of the word is trimmed

parts.note: an organ is a publication speaking for a group, i.e. a magazine, cut down to its first three letters
the setter Cyclops refers to himself, so I
Cal. is an abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A boast about the setter's organ, whose vasectomy is joked about again, and its effect on the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' looks anatomical after the clues about snipping, but it is the magazine Private Eye itself, where Cyclops sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabulous in its informal sense means wonderful or extraordinary, and magical carries the same enchanting, marvellous sense.

clue.text: Our vital statistics not so sensitive? Smashing!

definitions.note: the clue's 'Our' merely frames the statistics as the solver's own

parts.note: more numb, i.e. less able to feel
crunching something is smashing it up

explanation.surface: Our bust and hip measurements have lost their feeling, which is apparently great news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vital statistics' suggests body measurements; 'not so sensitive' must be read as more numb, so the first word is numb-er, not number.
explanation.definitionFit: Number crunching is large-scale processing of figures, which is how vital statistics such as births and deaths are produced.

clue.text: Silly old Cyclops faces having to get booze in

indicators.note: to get something in is to bring it inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: mug is slang for face
a spirit, an example of booze

explanation.surface: The foolish setter confronts having to buy the next round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition names the setter himself, because the word is used for oneself when made the fall guy: 'muggins here paid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggins is British slang for a fool, often said of oneself when stuck with an unwelcome task.

clue.text: Archer might well have one interbreed somewhere in London

parts.note: to cross breeds is to interbreed them
Bow is a district in London's East End

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer, the disgraced Tory novelist, might well have an affair somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Archer wants to be Jeffrey Archer, given the Eye's politics; it is simply a bowman.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbow is a mechanical bow fired by releasing a trigger, a weapon used by some archers.

clue.text: Sticks tool in Private Eye?

parts.note: to gum something is to stick it
a garden tool for weeding

explanation.surface: Is someone putting a tool into the pages of Private Eye magazine?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private Eye' looks like this magazine but is a private detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Gumshoe is American slang for a detective, from their quiet rubber-soled shoes, and a private eye is one.

clue.text: Cut-throat merchant? Go for it!

parts.note: surface reading: a ruthless trader
setter's reading: 'go for the' a throat vein, the idiom for attacking ruthlessly, with 'it' standing for the answer

explanation.walkthrough: A cut-throat would slash this throat vein, and the idiom 'go for the ...' means attack the weakest spot, so 'it' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The large neck veins are what a throat-cutter severs, and going for them means attacking an opponent's most vulnerable point.

clue.text: (& 26ac.) Labour seat-loser, Jim, quits (falsified holding account) — hard

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside
falsified things are doctored, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the standard abbreviation for account
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A Labour MP lost her seat after Jim quit amid fiddled expenses accounts, which is tough.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacqui Smith was Labour Home Secretary who lost her seat in 2010 after an expenses scandal, so 'falsified holding account' is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the Labour MP for Redditch, defeated at the 2010 general election after the parliamentary expenses scandal.

clue.text: Wishy-washy liberal at heart, Boris dismissed as to blame

indicators.note: something wishy-washy has no firm form, so these letters are reshaped
dismissed means sent away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the central letter of the five-letter name

explanation.surface: A feeble liberal privately thinks sacked Boris Johnson deserves the blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at heart' seems to describe the liberal, but it picks the middle of Boris, whose letter leaves before the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Being liable means being legally responsible, so the person liable is the one held to blame.

clue.text: Refuse female with piles early in the day

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for female
piles of something are lots of it
a.m. denotes the morning

explanation.surface: A woman with haemorrhoids says no to something in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb and 'piles' like the medical complaint; both are nouns here, rubbish and heaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Flotsam is wreckage or discarded rubbish floating on water, and refuse is a noun for rubbish.

clue.text: see 4dn.
As an orgasm is about temperature, etc., catching cold

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: relating to climate, which covers temperature, rainfall and so on
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A question about whether a sexual peak is about body heat, ruined by someone catching a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like C for circa, but the whole phrase is a description of one word. The definition is a phrase completed by an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgasm is a sexual climax, so it is by nature climactic, forming the culmination or peak.

clue.text: National player takes McKellen's lead, playing the Queen

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within

parts.note: a player picked for their country wins a cap, and is called a cap

indicators.note: the lead is what comes first, so the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the surname

explanation.surface: An actor at the National Theatre follows Ian McKellen in a royal role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National' suggests the National Theatre, but the player is a sports international. Queen is slang for a flamboyant gay man.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp means exaggeratedly theatrical and effeminate, the manner of someone playing up a queeny persona.

clue.text: see 20dn.
Woman's usual bust smothering Rex

indicators.note: to smother is to cover all round, so one piece goes inside
something bust is broken, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
R stands for Rex, king, as in royal ciphers

explanation.surface: A woman's typical bosom suffocates a dog called Rex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like the chest of the woman, but it means broken. 'Woman's' is 'Woman is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursula is a female given name, so it is one example of a woman.

clue.text: Ponce doesn't start to lie about being loutish

indicators.note: not starting means the opening letter is missing

parts.note: ponce is British slang for a pimp

indicators.note: about can mean around in a muddle, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A pimp who never starts lying is behaving like a yob.
explanation.walkthrough: Ponce in British slang means a pimp, though it is also used for an effete man.
explanation.definitionFit: Loutish behaviour is coarse and ill-mannered, which is what impolite describes in milder terms.
